newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Trade, fiscal woes sour Brazil '97 outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Trade, fiscal woes sour Brazil '97 outlook.

text.p: Having failed miserably this year to tame its fiscal beast, Brazil looks destined to resort to stop-and-go measures to steer the economy around a ballooning trade gap and other pitfalls lying ahead in 1997, analysts say.

Although economists see no crisis on the horizon, they say Brasilia will gain little ground next year on the fiscal front while it remains burdened by indebted states and committed to public sector wage hikes.
At the same time, it will not be able to ignore the country's widening trade deficit, which is growing surprisingly fast on relatively modest economic growth.
Import growth this year of 10 percent has dramatically outpaced economic growth of about 2.5 percent. And the trend has deteriorated sharply in recent months, economists say.

Brazil's trade accounts posted a surprisingly high $655 million gap in September and many economists say the deficit could widen another $1.0 billion in October. That could take the year-end deficit to about $4.0 billion, despite an original government target to end the year in equilibrium.
"They have to do something about the trade deficit. It is not a question of if, or whether, but when," said Marcelo Carvalho, J.P. Morgan's chief economist in Brazil.

Economists say an ever-expanding trade gap would put too much pressure on the current account, whose deficit now stands at 2.53 percent of gross domestic product. Such a scenario could invite frenzied market speculation on the overall effectiveness of Brazil's two-year-old anti-inflation drive.
The financial press has speculated that the Central Bank might tinker with foreign exchange policy to boost exports and reverse the worsening trend in trade accounts.
But economists say such a move would be unlikely, especially since the country's strong real currency is seen as a pillar of Brazil's successful anti-inflation fight.

Also, few see the government slapping on additional trade barriers, noting that Brasilia does not want to further irritate its trade partners following tariff hikes over the past two years on toy, auto and textile imports.
Instead, most Brazil watchers see a return to the micro-managing and stop-and-go measures that characterized economic policy-making in 1994-95.

"If you look at the business cycle of 1994-95 you might see a similar replay in 1996-97, with the government responding to a growth in imports with tighter monetary policy to control consumer demand," Carvalho said.
Most analysts said the government would probably wait until early next year to slow down the economy, which has seen a modest second-half recovery from a stagnant first half.

Economists say options available to policy-makers are limited because Brazil's stabilization plan has lacked sound fiscal discipline, which creates a more natural constraint on demand throughout the economy. And Brazil's fiscal situation -- clearly the biggest long-term worry among analysts -- is not likely to improve dramatically in 1997.

With economic reforms stalled in Congress, state government liabilities at 90 billion reais ($88 billion) and a public sector wage hike due next year, most observers do not expect a serious decline in the operational deficit, which is used by most economists to judge Brazil's fiscal performance.
After posting a surprisingly high operational deficit of 5.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1995, Brasilia pledged it would cut the figure in half over 1996.
Now the government is bracing for a figure closer to 3.8 percent and private economists are even more skeptical.

"Our projection for the aggregate public sector operational (deficit) is being revised from 3.5 percent to 4.5 percent of GDP -- a disappointing improvement if compared to last year's deficit of 5.0 percent of GDP," said ING Barings in a report released this week. "For 1997, the improvement should be small once again," ING said.

The bank said Brasilia's fiscal accounts will be pressured next year by poor fiscal performance by state governments; a slower reduction in real interest rates, which is bad news for the country's mammoth internal debt; only minor increases in revenues from state companies, and public sector wage hikes.
-- Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248-5414
